objectives: Explain clockwise ring ownership and why adding a node moves a subset of keys.
Distinguish virtual-node balance from hot-key traffic balance.
Compare ring placement, modulo hashing, and rendezvous placement without claiming migration safety.
retrieval: L063: why can hash(key)%N cause trouble when N changes?
L007: why do average arrival rates hide skew?

sections.title: Changing membership should not invalidate every address
sections.markdown:
A distributed cache uses hash(key)%3 to choose one of three nodes. Adding a fourth node changes the divisor for every key; many keys now map elsewhere. For a disposable cache, this causes a cold-miss surge. For authoritative data, changing the formula without moving and protecting data causes missing or misplaced writes.

Consistent hashing separates positions in a fixed hash space from the current membership count. Nodes occupy stable positions, and each key belongs to the next eligible position around the ring. Adding a position splits a neighboring ownership interval instead of changing the meaning of every hash. The placement rule reduces movement; it does not copy data, resolve concurrent writes, or prove safe failover.

sections.title: Walk clockwise, wrapping at the end
sections.markdown:
Hash each key into a fixed ordered space. Hash one or more node tokens into that same space. The first token at or clockwise after the key owns it; if no token is greater, wrap to the first. With tokens A=10, B=50, C=90 on a0–99 ring, keys11–50 belong to B,51–90 to C, and91–99 plus0–10 to A.

Add D=30. Keys11–30 move from B to D; the other intervals stay the same. Remove B instead and only B's former interval changes owner under this simple one-copy model. Exact moved fractions depend on token positions and the key distribution. With many roughly uniform tokens, expected movement approaches a balanced share, but a small sample or skew can differ substantially.

Virtual nodes give each physical node multiple token positions. They can smooth uneven intervals and let capacity be weighted by token count. The metadata and movement planning become more complex, and one physical failure affects all its virtual positions. Virtual nodes distribute many keys; they do not split the traffic to one viral key. Replication/failure-domain placement is an additional policy that must avoid treating multiple tokens on one machine as independent replicas.

sections.title: Executable ring membership change
sections.markdown:
The tiny ring below has chosen positions, not a cryptographic hash. It makes the interval movement inspectable. Production placement requires a stable shared hash/encoding, deterministic token identities, collision handling, and versioned membership.

```python
from bisect import bisect_left

def owner(point: int, tokens: dict[int, str]) -> str:
    positions = sorted(tokens)
    index = bisect_left(positions, point) % len(positions)
    return tokens[positions[index]]

before = {10: "A", 50: "B", 90: "C"}
after = {**before, 30: "D"}
moved = [p for p in range(100) if owner(p, before) != owner(p, after)]
assert moved == list(range(11, 31))
assert all(owner(p, after) == "D" for p in moved)
assert owner(99, after) == "A"
print(len(moved))
```

Expected output is20. Exactly20 of the100 integer positions move in this chosen example; it is not a universal25% guarantee when adding a fourth node. Open the academy's Mechanism lab to compare its fixed200-key virtual-node sample with modulo routing; the model declares its hash and node count.

Rendezvous hashing is a related alternative: score each (key,node) pair deterministically and choose the highest. Adding a node changes only keys for which the new node wins. It avoids explicit ring intervals but has a straightforward O(number of nodes) scoring cost unless optimized. P1's membership simulation uses that alternative; do not confuse a placement comparison with a real online resharding protocol.

sections.title: Placement agreement and data movement are separate
sections.markdown:
If two routers use different membership versions, they can disagree on the owner even with the same hash function. An authoritative shard should verify whether the request's ownership epoch is still acceptable; sending to a different address is not proof that the data is ready there. L067 studies copy, catch-up, handoff, and retirement.

A cache can often tolerate some placement churn, but a simultaneous cold set can overload its origin. Warm the new owner or bound fallback traffic according to the consistency contract. Do not solve this by silently reading random stale authoritative copies. Node weights should reflect capacity and failure-domain constraints, not just convenient names.

Common misconceptions: “consistent” means linearizable data, consistent hashing balances request frequency, virtual nodes are independent machines, and only1/N keys always move. The term concerns placement stability under membership changes. Correctness and availability still depend on the storage protocol and workload.

diagrams.caption: This is an interval ownership view of the0–99 ring, not a claim that the data moves automatically when the new token is published.
steps: Before the join, B owns keys just after A through50.
D takes only the interval just after A through30.
The rest of B’s interval and the other owners stay unchanged.
A separate protocol must move protected data before authoritative routing changes.

exercise.prompt: With ring tokens10=A,50=B,90=C, assign keys5,20,40,70,99. Add token30=D and identify exactly which listed keys change. Explain one failure caused by publishing new ownership before copying authoritative data.
rubric: Only key20 in the provided set moves to D.
Separate stable placement from copy/ownership correctness.
exercise.solution: Before:5→A,20→B,40→B,70→C,99→A. After adding D at30, only20 changes, now toD. Across all integer positions0–99,11–30 move. If routing changes first, a read for key20 may reach D before its value exists, or a write may reach D while B still accepts competing old-route writes. The ring reduced the set requiring a migration; it did not implement one. Use versioned placement and a handoff protocol with a verified ready target.

questions.prompt: “Consistent” in consistent hashing primarily refers to…
questions.explanation: The hash-placement property says nothing by itself about database consistency.

questions.prompt: In the0–99 ring example, adding D at30 moves how many integer key positions?
Do virtual nodes split requests for one identical hot key across many owners automatically?
questions.explanation: They spread token ranges/many keys; the same deterministic key still has its selected owner policy.

questions.prompt: Why might a new cache node harm the origin temporarily?
questions.answer: Remapped keys become cold, increasing misses and simultaneous origin work.
questions.explanation: Placement stability reduces movement but does not remove the cold-cache transition cost.

questions.answer: The node with the highest deterministic score for the key-node pair.
questions.explanation: It is a placement alternative; its scoring and membership policy still need stable shared definitions.

flashcards.back: First eligible clockwise token, wrapping at the end.
The ownership interval that the new token takes from its successor.
Spread many key ranges and express capacity weights.
No. Placement stability and data-consistency protocols are different.
Requires versioned routing and data handoff beyond the placement function.

mentalModel: Keep the address space stable, move only affected ownership, and prove data handoff separately.
